claim: Engaging with vocal sounds is critical for children's social-emotional learning.
source: Engaging with vocal sounds is critical for children's social-emotional learning, and children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) often 'tune out' voices in their environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on voice processing and social-emotional learning.

claim: Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) often 'tune out' voices in their environment.
source: Engaging with vocal sounds is critical for children's social-emotional learning, and children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) often 'tune out' voices in their environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations in the manuscript to prior research on ASD and voice processing.

claim: Social communication abilities in children with ASD are related to activation in key structures of reward and salience processing regions during voice processing.
source: We examined neural responses elicited by unfamiliar voices and mother's voice, a biologically salient voice for social learning, and identified a striking relationship between social communication abilities in children with ASD and activation in key structures of reward and salience processing regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from fMRI analysis showing correlations between brain activation and social communication scores.

claim: Functional connectivity between voice-selective and reward regions during voice processing predicted social communication in children with ASD.
source: Functional connectivity between voice-selective and reward regions during voice processing predicted social communication in children with ASD and distinguished them from typically developing children.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from functional connectivity analysis and support vector regression.

claim: Functional connectivity between voice-selective and reward regions during voice processing distinguished children with ASD from typically developing children.
source: Functional connectivity between voice-selective and reward regions during voice processing predicted social communication in children with ASD and distinguished them from typically developing children.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from support vector classification analysis.

claim: Results support the Social Motivation Theory of ASD by showing reward system deficits associated with the processing of mother's voice in children with ASD.
source: Results support the Social Motivation Theory of ASD by showing reward system deficits associated with the processing of a critical social stimulus, mother's voice, in children with ASD.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental findings in the context of existing theory.

claim: Engaging with vocal sounds is important for language during typical development.
source: The human voice is a critical social stimulus in children's environment, and engaging with vocal sounds is important for language (Kuhl et al., 2005a; Christophe et al., 1994) and social-emotional learning (DeCasper and Fifer, 1980) during typical development.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Engaging with vocal sounds is important for social-emotional learning during typical development.
source: The human voice is a critical social stimulus in children's environment, and engaging with vocal sounds is important for language (Kuhl et al., 2005a; Christophe et al., 1994) and social-emotional learning (DeCasper and Fifer, 1980) during typical development.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are often not responsive to voices.
source: However, children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are often not responsive to voices (Kanner, 1968; Harstad et al., 2016), and it has been hypothesized that voice processing deficits contribute to pronounced social communication difficulties in ASD (Klin, 1991; Kuhl et al., 2005b; Whitehouse and Bishop, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Voice processing deficits contribute to pronounced social communication difficulties in ASD.
source: However, children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are often not responsive to voices (Kanner, 1968; Harstad et al., 2016), and it has been hypothesized that voice processing deficits contribute to pronounced social communication difficulties in ASD (Klin, 1991; Kuhl et al., 2005b; Whitehouse and Bishop, 2008).
evidence: This claim is presented as a hypothesis supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Children with ASD have a deficit in processing mother's voice.
source: A special case of voice processing impairments in children with ASD is a deficit in processing mother's voice (Klin, 1991), a biologically salient and implicitly rewarding sound for typically developing (TD) children (Lamb, 1981; Thoman et al., 1977), which is closely associated with cognitive (Kuhl et al., 2005a; Christophe et al., 1994) and social development (DeCasper and Fifer, 1980; Adams and Passman, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Mother's voice is a biologically salient and implicitly rewarding sound for typically developing (TD) children.
source: A special case of voice processing impairments in children with ASD is a deficit in processing mother's voice (Klin, 1991), a biologically salient and implicitly rewarding sound for typically developing (TD) children (Lamb, 1981; Thoman et al., 1977), which is closely associated with cognitive (Kuhl et al., 2005a; Christophe et al., 1994) and social development (DeCasper and Fifer, 1980; Adams and Passman, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mother's voice is closely associated with cognitive development.
source: A special case of voice processing impairments in children with ASD is a deficit in processing mother's voice (Klin, 1991), a biologically salient and implicitly rewarding sound for typically developing (TD) children (Lamb, 1981; Thoman et al., 1977), which is closely associated with cognitive (Kuhl et al., 2005a; Christophe et al., 1994) and social development (DeCasper and Fifer, 1980; Adams and Passman, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Mother's voice is closely associated with social development.
source: A special case of voice processing impairments in children with ASD is a deficit in processing mother's voice (Klin, 1991), a biologically salient and implicitly rewarding sound for typically developing (TD) children (Lamb, 1981; Thoman et al., 1977), which is closely associated with cognitive (Kuhl et al., 2005a; Christophe et al., 1994) and social development (DeCasper and Fifer, 1980; Adams and Passman, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Very little is known regarding the neurobiology of voice processing networks in children with ASD.
source: Compared to studies of visual face processing (Dalton et al., 2005; Dawson et al., 2002; Dichter et al., 2012; Pierce et al., 2001; Schultz et al., 2000), very little is known regarding the neurobiology of voice processing networks in children with ASD, which is fundamental to human communication.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research and represents a gap in the literature.

claim: It remains unknown why children with ASD often do not engage with the voices in their environment.
source: It remains unknown why children with ASD often do not engage with the voices in their environment.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: It is not known which aspects of voice processing are impaired in children with ASD.
source: Specifically, it is not known which aspects of voice processing are impaired in children with ASD.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Sensory deficits may negatively affect voice processing and contribute to social communication deficits in ASD.
source: One possibility is that sensory deficits negatively affect voice processing and contribute to social communication deficits (Dinstein et al., 2012; Markram et al., 2007; Russo et al., 2010; Marco et al., 2011; Leekam et al., 2007; Woynaroski et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is presented as a possibility supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The social motivation theory of ASD posits that impairments in representing the reward value of human vocal sounds impedes individuals with ASD from engaging with these stimuli.
source: The social motivation theory of ASD posits that impairments in representing the reward value of human vocal sounds impedes individuals with ASD from engaging with these stimuli, and contributes to social interaction difficulties (Dawson et al., 2002; Chevallier et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim describes a theoretical framework supported by citations.

claim: Impairments in representing the reward value of human vocal sounds contributes to social interaction difficulties in ASD.
source: The social motivation theory of ASD posits that impairments in representing the reward value of human vocal sounds impedes individuals with ASD from engaging with these stimuli, and contributes to social interaction difficulties (Dawson et al., 2002; Chevallier et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim describes a theoretical framework supported by citations.

claim: There has been a dearth of compelling experimental evidence showing aberrant reward processing in response to clinically meaningful social stimuli in ASD.
source: While this is a prominent model for considering social communication function in ASD, there has been a dearth of compelling experimental evidence showing aberrant reward processing in response to clinically meaningful social stimuli (Clements et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim represents a gap in the literature supported by a citation.

claim: The social motivation theory posits that individuals with ASD show reduced engagement and connectivity in the mesolimbic reward system during social processing.
source: For example, the social motivation theory posits that individuals with ASD show reduced engagement and connectivity in the mesolimbic reward system, including the ventral tegmental area (VTA), nucleus accumbens (NAc), orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), and structures of the salience and affective processing systems, instantiated in the anterior insula and amygdala, during social processing (Chevallier et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim describes a theoretical framework supported by a citation.

claim: Adults with ASD show reduced regional activity in voice-selective superior temporal sulcus (STS).
source: Previous brain imaging research of voice processing in adults with ASD has supported the sensory deficit model by showing reduced regional activity in voice-selective superior temporal sulcus (STS) (Gervais et al., 2004; Schelinski et al., 2016), a core region associated with structural analysis of the human voice (Belin et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Superior temporal sulcus (STS) is a core region associated with structural analysis of the human voice.
source: Previous brain imaging research of voice processing in adults with ASD has supported the sensory deficit model by showing reduced regional activity in voice-selective superior temporal sulcus (STS) (Gervais et al., 2004; Schelinski et al., 2016), a core region associated with structural analysis of the human voice (Belin et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: There have been few studies examining voice processing in ASD, particularly when compared to the extensive face processing literature.
source: First, there have been few studies examining voice processing in ASD, particularly when compared to the extensive face processing literature (Dalton et al., 2005; Dichter et al., 2012; Pierce et al., 2001; Schultz et al., 2000; Baron-Cohen et al., 1999; Dapretto et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim represents a gap in the literature supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies have not employed biologically salient voices to probe brain circuit function in children with ASD.
source: Second, previous studies have not employed biologically salient voices (e.g. mother/caregiver), which are thought to be implicitly rewarding (Chevallier et al., 2012), to probe brain circuit function in children with ASD.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in the literature.

claim: Mother's voice elicits activation within voice-selective, mesolimbic reward, affective, and salience, and face-processing brain regions in TD children.
source: For example, a recent study in TD children showed that, compared to unfamiliar voices, mother's voice elicits activation within voice-selective, mesolimbic reward, affective, and salience, and face-processing brain regions, and connectivity between these regions predicts social communication abilities (Abrams et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Connectivity between voice-selective, mesolimbic reward, affective, and salience, and face-processing brain regions predicts social communication abilities in TD children.
source: For example, a recent study in TD children showed that, compared to unfamiliar voices, mother's voice elicits activation within voice-selective, mesolimbic reward, affective, and salience, and face-processing brain regions, and connectivity between these regions predicts social communication abilities (Abrams et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Previous studies of voice processing have focused on group differences in brain activity between individuals with ASD and matched controls but have not examined how individual variation in social communication abilities are associated with social brain circuit function in ASD.
source: Third, previous studies of voice processing have focused on group differences in brain activity between individuals with ASD and matched controls but have not examined how individual variation in social communication abilities are associated with social brain circuit function in ASD.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in the literature.

claim: Autism has been conceptualized as a disorder of brain connectivity.
source: Finally, although autism has been conceptualized as a disorder of brain connectivity (Uddin et al., 2013a; Wass, 2011), previous brain imaging studies of human voice processing in ASD have focused on regional activation profiles in voice-selective cortex (Gervais et al., 2004; Schelinski et al., 2016) and have not employed a brain networks perspective.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Previous brain imaging studies of human voice processing in ASD have focused on regional activation profiles in voice-selective cortex and have not employed a brain networks perspective.
source: Finally, although autism has been conceptualized as a disorder of brain connectivity (Uddin et al., 2013a; Wass, 2011), previous brain imaging studies of human voice processing in ASD have focused on regional activation profiles in voice-selective cortex (Gervais et al., 2004; Schelinski et al., 2016) and have not employed a brain networks perspective.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in the literature supported by citations.

claim: Children with ASD have reduced intrinsic connectivity between voice-selective STS and key structures of the mesolimbic reward system, anterior insula, and amygdala.
source: For example, a previous resting state fMRI study investigated intrinsic connectivity of voice-selective cortex and showed that children with ASD have reduced connectivity between voice-selective STS and key structures of the mesolimbic reward system, anterior insula, and amygdala (Abrams et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The strength of intrinsic connectivity between voice-selective STS and reward/salience regions predicted social communication abilities in children with ASD.
source: Moreover, the strength of intrinsic connectivity in this network predicted social communication abilities in children with ASD.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (implied from context).

claim: Children with ASD show reduced activity in right hemisphere planum polare (PP) in response to unfamiliar female voices compared to TD children.
source: Direct group comparisons between TD children and children with ASD in response to unfamiliar female voices show that children with ASD have reduced activity in a relatively small set of brain regions confined to lateral temporal cortex (Figure 2A; see Appendix 1—table 1 for effect sizes and Appendix 1—figure 2 for within-group results). Specifically, children with ASD show reduced activity in right hemisphere planum polare (PP), an area of auditory association cortex within the superior temporal gyrus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fMRI data and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TD children have greater activity for unfamiliar female voices, compared to environmental sounds, in right hemisphere planum polare.
source: Within-group signal level analysis showed that TD children have greater activity for unfamiliar female voices, compared to environmental sounds, in this brain region (i.e. positive βs; see Appendix 1—figure 3A) while children with ASD show weaker activity for this same contrast (i.e. negative βs for unfamiliar voices compared to environmental sounds).
evidence: This claim is supported by signal level analysis data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3A.

claim: Children with ASD show weaker activity for unfamiliar voices compared to environmental sounds in right hemisphere planum polare.
source: Within-group signal level analysis showed that TD children have greater activity for unfamiliar female voices, compared to environmental sounds, in this brain region (i.e. positive βs; see Appendix 1—figure 3A) while children with ASD show weaker activity for this same contrast (i.e. negative βs for unfamiliar voices compared to environmental sounds).
evidence: This claim is supported by signal level analysis data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3A.

claim: No brain regions showed greater activity for unfamiliar female voices in the ASD group compared to the TD group.
source: No brain regions showed greater activity for unfamiliar female voices in the ASD, compared to the TD, group.
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of significant findings in the fMRI analysis.

claim: TD children show greater activity in several visual processing regions in response to mother's voice compared to children with ASD.
source: Direct group comparisons between brain responses measured from TD children and children with ASD in response to mother's voice relative to unfamiliar female voices revealed that children with ASD have reduced activity in several visual processing regions as well as key structures of the medial temporal lobe memory system (Figure 2B; see Appendix 1—table 1 for effect sizes and Appendix 1—figure 4 for within-group results). Specifically, whole-brain analysis revealed that TD children had greater activation compared to children with ASD for mother's voice in bilateral intercalcarine cortex extending into lingual gyrus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fMRI data and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Children with ASD show reduced activity in bilateral intercalcarine cortex extending into lingual gyrus in response to mother's voice compared to TD children.
source: Specifically, whole-brain analysis revealed that TD children had greater activation compared to children with ASD for mother's voice in bilateral intercalcarine cortex extending into lingual gyrus.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fMRI data.

claim: Children with ASD showed reduced activity in fusiform gyrus bilaterally in response to mother's voice compared to TD children.
source: Moreover, children with ASD showed reduced activity compared to TD children in a broad extent of fusiform gyrus bilaterally, including both left-hemisphere occipital regions of fusiform as well as temporal occipital regions in the right-hemisphere.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fMRI data.

claim: Children with ASD showed less activity for mother's voice in right-hemisphere posterior hippocampus compared to TD children.
source: Children with ASD also showed less activity for mother's voice in right-hemisphere posterior hippocampus, a critical region for learning and memory, as well as precuneus cortex of the default mode network.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fMRI data.

claim: Right-hemisphere posterior hippocampus is a critical region for learning and memory.
source: Children with ASD also showed less activity for mother's voice in right-hemisphere posterior hippocampus, a critical region for learning and memory, as well as precuneus cortex of the default mode network.
evidence: This claim is based on established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: TD children have greater activity for mother's voice compared to unfamiliar female voices in visual processing and memory regions.
source: Signal level analysis shows that TD children have greater activity for mother's voice compared to unfamiliar female voices in these brain regions (i.e. positive βs; see Appendix 1—figure 3B) while children with ASD show weaker activity for mother's voice (i.e. negative βs).
evidence: This claim is supported by signal level analysis data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3B.

claim: Children with ASD show weaker activity for mother's voice compared to unfamiliar female voices in visual processing and memory regions.
source: Signal level analysis shows that TD children have greater activity for mother's voice compared to unfamiliar female voices in these brain regions (i.e. positive βs; see Appendix 1—figure 3B) while children with ASD show weaker activity for mother's voice (i.e. negative βs).
evidence: This claim is supported by signal level analysis data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3B.

claim: No brain structures showed greater activity for mother's voice in the ASD group compared to the TD group.
source: No brain structures showed greater activity for mother's voice in the ASD, compared to the TD, group.
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of significant findings in the fMRI analysis.

claim: Social communication scores are correlated with activity strength during unfamiliar female voice processing in auditory association cortex, the NAc of the reward system, and AI of the salience network in children with ASD.
source: Results from this analysis show a striking pattern: the strength of activity in a variety of brain systems serving auditory, reward, and salience detection is correlated with social communication abilities in children with ASD (Figure 3A; see Appendix 1—table 2 for effect sizes). Specifically, this pattern was apparent in auditory association cortex of the superior temporal plane, including the PP, but also in the nucleus accumbens of the reward pathway, and anterior insula of the salience network.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fMRI data and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Greater social function in children with ASD is associated with greater brain activity in auditory, reward, and salience processing regions during unfamiliar voice processing.
source: Scatterplots show that brain activity and social communication abilities vary across a range of values and greater social function, reflected by lower social communication scores, is associated with greater brain activity in these auditory, reward, and salience processing regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fMRI data and correlation analysis.

claim: The strength of activity in auditory, reward, and salience regions during unfamiliar voice processing was a reliable predictor of social communication function in children with ASD.
source: Support vector regression (SVR) analysis (Abrams et al., 2016; Cohen et al., 2010) showed that the strength of activity in these regions was a reliable predictor of social communication function in these children (R ≥ 0.49; p ≤ 0.011 for all regions).
evidence: This claim is supported by support vector regression analysis of experimental data.

claim: Social communication scores are correlated with activity strength during mother's voice processing in primary auditory and association cortex, voice-selective STS, vmPFC of the reward system, AI and rACC of the salience network, and SMA in children with ASD.
source: We next examined the question of heterogeneity in the context of mother's voice processing, and results show a similar pattern: children with ASD with greater social communication abilities showed greater activation for mother's voice in a wide extent of primary auditory, auditory association, and voice-selective cortex as well as mesolimbic reward, salience detection, and motor regions (Figure 3B). Specifically, this brain-behavior relationship was evident in auditory regions of superior temporal cortex, including medial aspects of bilateral Heschl's gyrus, which contains primary auditory cortex, right-hemisphere PP of the superior temporal plane, as well as bilateral voice-selective mSTS. This relationship was also observed in regions of the salience network, including dorsal aspects of AI bilaterally and right-hemisphere rostral ACC (rACC), as well as vmPFC of the reward network.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fMRI data and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The strength of activity in specific brain regions during mother's voice processing was a reliable predictor of social communication function in children with ASD.
source: SVR results indicated that the strength of activity in these particular brain regions during mother's voice processing was a reliable predictor of social communication function in these children (R ≥ 0.50; p ≤ 0.009 for all regions).
evidence: This claim is supported by support vector regression analysis of experimental data.

claim: There were no univariate group differences in individual connectivity links during unfamiliar voice processing after correcting for multiple comparisons.
source: There were no univariate group differences in individual links during either unfamiliar voice (Figure 4B) or mother's voice processing (Figure 4C) after correcting for multiple comparisons (FDR, q < 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional connectivity analysis of experimental data.

claim: There were no univariate group differences in individual connectivity links during mother's voice processing after correcting for multiple comparisons.
source: There were no univariate group differences in individual links during either unfamiliar voice (Figure 4B) or mother's voice processing (Figure 4C) after correcting for multiple comparisons (FDR, q < 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by functional connectivity analysis of experimental data.

claim: Multivariate connectivity patterns during unfamiliar voice processing were unable to predict group membership above chance.
source: Support vector classification (SVC) results showed that multivariate connectivity patterns during unfamiliar voice processing were unable to predict group membership above chance (SVC Accuracy = 51.6%, p = 0.31); however, multivariate connectivity patterns during mother's voice processing accurately predicted TD vs. ASD group membership (SVC Accuracy = 70.4%, p = 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by support vector classification analysis of experimental data.

claim: Multivariate connectivity patterns during mother's voice processing accurately predicted TD vs. ASD group membership.
source: Support vector classification (SVC) results showed that multivariate connectivity patterns during unfamiliar voice processing were unable to predict group membership above chance (SVC Accuracy = 51.6%, p = 0.31); however, multivariate connectivity patterns during mother's voice processing accurately predicted TD vs. ASD group membership (SVC Accuracy = 70.4%, p = 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by support vector classification analysis of experimental data.

claim: Patterns of brain connectivity during biologically-salient voice processing, but not unfamiliar voice processing, can distinguish children with ASD from TD children.
source: Results show that patterns of brain connectivity during biologically-salient voice processing, but not unfamiliar voice processing, can distinguish children with ASD from TD children.
evidence: This claim is supported by support vector classification analysis of experimental data.

claim: There were no significant univariate correlations between the strength of brain connectivity during unfamiliar voice processing and social communication abilities in children with ASD.
source: We next examined the relation between connectivity beta weights in each cell of the connectivity matrix and social communication scores in children with ASD. There were no significant univariate correlations between the strength of brain connectivity during either unfamiliar (Figure 5B) or mother's voice processing (Figure 5C) and social communication abilities.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: There were no significant univariate correlations between the strength of brain connectivity during mother's voice processing and social communication abilities in children with ASD.
source: We next examined the relation between connectivity beta weights in each cell of the connectivity matrix and social communication scores in children with ASD. There were no significant univariate correlations between the strength of brain connectivity during either unfamiliar (Figure 5B) or mother's voice processing (Figure 5C) and social communication abilities.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: Multivariate connectivity patterns during unfamiliar and mother's voice processing accurately predict social communication scores in children with ASD.
source: SVR results showed that multivariate connectivity patterns during unfamiliar and mother's voice processing accurately predict social communication scores in children with ASD (R = 0.42, p = 0.015).
evidence: This claim is supported by support vector regression analysis of experimental data.

claim: There is a striking relationship between individuals' social communication abilities and the strength of activation in reward and salience processing brain regions during human voice processing in children with ASD.
source: Here, we identify a striking relationship between individuals' social communication abilities and the strength of activation in reward and salience processing brain regions, notably NAc and AI, during human voice processing in children with ASD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fMRI data.

claim: Multivariate connectivity patterns within an extended voice processing network distinguished children with ASD from their TD peers.
source: Multivariate connectivity patterns within an extended voice processing network distinguished children with ASD from their TD peers and predicted social communication abilities in children with ASD.
evidence: This claim is supported by support vector classification analysis of experimental data.

claim: Multivariate connectivity patterns within an extended voice processing network predicted social communication abilities in children with ASD.
source: Multivariate connectivity patterns within an extended voice processing network distinguished children with ASD from their TD peers and predicted social communication abilities in children with ASD.
evidence: This claim is supported by support vector regression analysis of experimental data.

claim: Dysfunction of the brain's reward system provides a stable brain signature of ASD that contributes to aberrant processing of salient vocal information.
source: These findings suggest that dysfunction of the brain's reward system provides a stable brain signature of ASD that contributes to aberrant processing of salient vocal information (Abrams et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental findings supported by a citation.

claim: Both regional and network features associated with voice processing predicted social function in children with ASD.
source: Our findings showed that both regional and network features associated with voice processing, encompassing voice-selective cortex in the STS and extended voice-processing network that includes auditory, reward, and salience regions, predicted social function in children with ASD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fMRI data.

claim: Social communication function is a unifying factor for explaining regional activation profiles and large-scale connectivity patterns linking key elements of the social brain.
source: We suggest that social communication function – human's ability to interact with and relate to others – is a unifying factor for explaining regional activation profiles and large-scale connectivity patterns linking key elements of the social brain.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Voice-related network function during the processing of a clinically and biologically meaningful social stimulus predicts both ASD group membership as well as social communication abilities in children with ASD.
source: We show that voice-related network function during the processing of a clinically and biologically meaningful social stimulus predicts both ASD group membership as well as social communication abilities in these children.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fMRI data.

claim: Brief samples of a biologically salient voice, mother's voice, elicit a distinct neural signature in children with ASD.
source: Our results demonstrate that brief samples of a biologically salient voice, mother's voice, elicit a distinct neural signature in children with ASD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fMRI data.

claim: Typically developing children prefer biologically salient voices such as a mother's voice which provide critical cues for social and language learning.
source: Specifically, typically developing children prefer biologically salient voices such as a mother's voice which provide critical cues for social (Adams and Passman, 1979) and language learning (Liu et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Children with ASD do not show a preference for biologically salient voices.
source: In contrast, both anecdotal (Kanner, 1968) and experimental accounts (Klin, 1991) indicate that children with ASD do not show a preference for these sounds.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Aberrant function within the extended voice processing network may underlie insensitivity to biologically salient voices in children with ASD.
source: We suggest that aberrant function within the extended voice processing network may underlie insensitivity to biologically salient voices in children with ASD, which may subsequently affect key developmental processes associated with social and pragmatic language learning.

claim: Insensitivity to biologically salient voices may affect key developmental processes associated with social and pragmatic language learning in children with ASD.

claim: Early attraction to vocal cues may be a critical step in a developmental process that includes speech sound discrimination, mimicry, and, ultimately, language learning and verbal communication.

claim: Network connectivity of an extended voice-selective network distinguished ASD and TD children.
source: Moreover, network connectivity of an extended voice-selective network, which includes nodes of the salience and reward networks, distinguished ASD and TD children and predicted social communication abilities in children with ASD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fMRI data.

claim: Network connectivity of an extended voice-selective network predicted social communication abilities in children with ASD.
source: Moreover, network connectivity of an extended voice-selective network, which includes nodes of the salience and reward networks, distinguished ASD and TD children and predicted social communication abilities in children with ASD.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fMRI data.

claim: These results are the first to show that aberrant function of reward circuitry during voice processing is a distinguishing feature of childhood autism.
source: These results are the first to show that aberrant function of reward circuitry during voice processing is a distinguishing feature of childhood autism, and may limit the ability of children with ASD to experience vocal sounds as rewarding or salient.

claim: Aberrant function of reward circuitry during voice processing may limit the ability of children with ASD to experience vocal sounds as rewarding or salient.
source: These results are the first to show that aberrant function of reward circuitry during voice processing is a distinguishing feature of childhood autism, and may limit the ability of children with ASD to experience vocal sounds as rewarding or salient.
evidence: This claim is a speculative inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Functional connectivity between voice-selective STS and reward and salience processing regions is an important predictor of social skill development in children.
source: Our findings add to a growing literature suggesting that functional connectivity between voice-selective STS and reward and salience processing regions is an important predictor of social skill development in children (Abrams et al., 2016; Abrams et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to prior research.

claim: Clinical efforts to increase the reward value of vocal interactions in children with ASD may be key to remediating social communication deficits in these individuals.
source: Findings suggest that clinical efforts to increase the reward value of vocal interactions in children with ASD may be key to remediating social communication deficits in these individuals.
evidence: This claim is a speculative inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Neural activity and connectivity measures may represent a quantitative metric for assessing response to clinical treatments focused on verbal interactions.
source: Furthermore, neural activity and connectivity measures may represent a quantitative metric for assessing response to clinical treatments focused on verbal interactions.
evidence: This claim is a speculative inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The sample size is relatively modest compared to recent task-based brain imaging studies of neurotypical adult populations and resting-state fMRI or structural MRI studies in individuals with ASD.
source: First, the sample size is relatively modest compared to recent task-based brain imaging studies of neurotypical adult populations and resting-state fMRI or structural MRI studies in individuals with ASD, however these types of studies do not face the same data collection challenges as task-based studies in clinical pediatric populations (Yerys et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is an acknowledgment of a study limitation.

claim: Resting-state and structural imaging studies are unable to address specific questions related to social information processing in ASD.
source: Importantly, resting-state and structural imaging studies are unable to address specific questions related to social information processing in ASD, such as biologically salient voice processing, which are critical for understanding the brain bases of social dysfunction in affected children.
evidence: This claim is based on methodological considerations.

claim: The sample size is larger than, or comparable to, the majority of task-fMRI studies in children with ASD published since 2017.
source: Indeed, our sample size is larger than, or comparable to, the majority of task-fMRI studies in children with ASD published since 2017, and have more stringent individual-level sampling compared to these studies.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison with the literature.

claim: Modest sample sizes yield highly replicable results with only four runs of task data with a similar number of trials per run.
source: A recent report examining this question showed that modest sample sizes, comparable to those described in our submitted manuscript, yield highly replicable results with only four runs of task data with a similar number of trials per run as our study (Nee, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Each child participant had at least seven functional imaging runs of the event-related fMRI task that met strict head movement criteria.
source: In comparison, we required that each child participant had at least seven functional imaging runs of our event-related fMRI task that met our strict head movement criteria.
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology.

claim: The study was unable to include lower functioning children with ASD since the scanner environment is ill-suited for these children.
source: A final limitation of this work is that, consistent with the vast majority of brain imaging studies in children with ASD, we were unable to include lower functioning children with ASD since the scanner environment is ill-suited for these children (Yerys et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is an acknowledgment of a study limitation supported by a citation.

claim: Activity profiles and network connectivity patterns within voice-selective and reward regions, measured during unfamiliar and mother's voice processing, distinguish children with ASD from TD peers.
source: Results show that activity profiles and network connectivity patterns within voice-selective and reward regions, measured during unfamiliar and mother's voice processing, distinguish children with ASD from TD peers and predict their social communication abilities.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fMRI data.

claim: Activity profiles and network connectivity patterns within voice-selective and reward regions predict social communication abilities in children with ASD.
source: Results show that activity profiles and network connectivity patterns within voice-selective and reward regions, measured during unfamiliar and mother's voice processing, distinguish children with ASD from TD peers and predict their social communication abilities.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental fMRI data.

claim: These findings are consistent with the social motivation theory of ASD by linking human voice processing to dysfunction in the brain's reward centers.
source: These findings are consistent with the social motivation theory of ASD by linking human voice processing to dysfunction in the brain's reward centers, and have implications for the treatment of social communication deficits in children with ASD.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental findings in the context of theory.

claim: Parent training has emerged as a powerful and cost-effective approach for increasing treatment intensity.
source: For example, parent training has emerged as a powerful and cost-effective approach for increasing treatment intensity (National Research Council, 2001): treatment delivery in the child's natural environment promotes functional communication (Delprato, 2001), generalization (Stokes and Baer, 1977), and maintenance of skills over time (Sheinkopf and Siegel, 1998; Moes and Frea, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Treatment delivery in the child's natural environment promotes functional communication.
source: For example, parent training has emerged as a powerful and cost-effective approach for increasing treatment intensity (National Research Council, 2001): treatment delivery in the child's natural environment promotes functional communication (Delprato, 2001), generalization (Stokes and Baer, 1977), and maintenance of skills over time (Sheinkopf and Siegel, 1998; Moes and Frea, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Treatment delivery in the child's natural environment promotes generalization.
source: For example, parent training has emerged as a powerful and cost-effective approach for increasing treatment intensity (National Research Council, 2001): treatment delivery in the child's natural environment promotes functional communication (Delprato, 2001), generalization (Stokes and Baer, 1977), and maintenance of skills over time (Sheinkopf and Siegel, 1998; Moes and Frea, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Treatment delivery in the child's natural environment promotes maintenance of skills over time.
source: For example, parent training has emerged as a powerful and cost-effective approach for increasing treatment intensity (National Research Council, 2001): treatment delivery in the child's natural environment promotes functional communication (Delprato, 2001), generalization (Stokes and Baer, 1977), and maintenance of skills over time (Sheinkopf and Siegel, 1998; Moes and Frea, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A child's ability to focus on, and direct neural resources to, critical communication partners may be a key to improving social function in affected children.
source: Findings from the current study, which demonstrate a link between social communication function and neural processing of mother's voice, support the importance of parent training by suggesting that a child's ability to focus on, and direct neural resources to, these critical communication partners may be a key to improving social function in affected children.
evidence: This claim is a speculative inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: All children were required to be right-handed and have a full-scale IQ > 80.
source: All children were required to be right-handed and have a full-scale IQ > 80, as measured by the Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence (WASI) (Wechsler, 1999).
evidence: This claim describes the study inclusion criteria.

claim: 28 children met ASD criteria based on an algorithm that combines information from both the module 3 of the ADOS-2 and the ADI–Revised.
source: 28 children met ASD criteria based on an algorithm (Risi et al., 2006) that combines information from both the module 3 of the ADOS-2 (47) and the ADI–Revised (Lord et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim describes the study sample and diagnostic criteria.

claim: Children in the ASD sample are considered 'high-functioning' and had fluent language skills and above-average reading skills.
source: Importantly, children in the ASD sample are considered 'high-functioning' and had fluent language skills and above-average reading skills (Table 1).
evidence: This claim describes the study sample characteristics shown in Table 1.

claim: Children in the ASD sample are generally characterized as having communication impairments, especially in the area of reciprocal conversation.
source: Nevertheless, these children are generally characterized as having communication impairments, especially in the area of reciprocal conversation.
evidence: This claim describes the study sample characteristics.

claim: The final TD and ASD groups consisted of 21 children in each group who were matched for full-scale IQ, age, sex, and head motion during the fMRI scan.
source: The final TD and ASD groups that were included in the analysis consisted of 21 children in each group who were matched for full-scale IQ, age, sex, and head motion during the fMRI scan (Table 1).
evidence: This claim describes the study sample and matching criteria shown in Table 1.

claim: All participants are the biological offspring of the mothers whose voices were used in this study.
source: All participants are the biological offspring of the mothers whose voices were used in this study (i.e. none of our participants were adopted, and therefore none of the mother's voices are from an adoptive mother), and all participants were raised in homes that included their mothers.
evidence: This claim describes the study sample characteristics.

claim: Auditory stimuli were presented in 10 separate runs, each lasting 4 min.
source: Auditory stimuli were presented in 10 separate runs, each lasting 4 min.
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology.

claim: One run consisted of 56 trials of mother's voice, unfamiliar female voices, environmental sounds and catch trials, which were pseudo-randomly ordered within each run.
source: One run consisted of 56 trials of mother's voice, unfamiliar female voices, environmental sounds and catch trials, which were pseudo-randomly ordered within each run.
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology.

claim: Catch trial accuracies were similar between TD and ASD groups.
source: Although the button box failed to register responses during data collection in four children with ASD and nine TD children, data analysis of the catch trails for 17 children with ASD and 12 TD children showed similar catch trial accuracies between TD (accuracy = 91%) and ASD groups (accuracy = 89%; two-sample t-test results: t(2) = 0.35, p = 0.73).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental behavioral data.

claim: A total of 48 exemplars of each stimulus condition were presented to each subject across the ten runs.
source: Across the ten runs, a total of 48 exemplars of each stimulus condition were presented to each subject (i.e. 144 total exemplars produced by each of the three vocal sources, including the child's mother, unfamiliar female voice #1, and unfamiliar female voice #2).
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology.

claim: All stimuli were presented at a sound level of 75 dBA.
source: Headphone sound levels were calibrated prior to each data collection session, and all stimuli were presented at a sound level of 75 dBA.
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology.

claim: Participants were scanned using an event-related design.
source: Participants were scanned using an event-related design.
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology.

claim: Auditory stimuli were presented during silent intervals between volume acquisitions to eliminate the effects of scanner noise on auditory discrimination.
source: Auditory stimuli were presented during silent intervals between volume acquisitions to eliminate the effects of scanner noise on auditory discrimination.
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology and its rationale.

claim: All 42 participants included in the analysis had at least seven functional runs that met movement criteria.
source: All 42 participants included in the analysis had at least seven functional runs that met our movement criteria, and the total number of runs included for TD and ASD groups were similar (TD = 192 runs; ASD = 188 runs).
evidence: This claim describes the study data quality.

claim: The total number of runs included for TD and ASD groups were similar.
source: All 42 participants included in the analysis had at least seven functional runs that met our movement criteria, and the total number of runs included for TD and ASD groups were similar (TD = 192 runs; ASD = 188 runs).
evidence: This claim describes the study data quality.

claim: Significant clusters of activation were determined using a voxel-wise statistical height threshold of p < 0.005, with family-wise error corrections for multiple spatial comparisons (p < 0.05; 67 voxels).
source: Significant clusters of activation were determined using a voxel-wise statistical height threshold of p < 0.005, with family-wise error corrections for multiple spatial comparisons (p < 0.05; 67 voxels) determined using Monte Carlo simulations (Forman et al., 1995; Ward, 2000) using a custom Matlab script (see Source Code).
evidence: This claim describes the study statistical methods.

claim: Functional connectivity was examined using a generalized psychophysiological interaction (gPPI) model within an extended voice processing brain network defined a priori from intrinsic connectivity results described in a previous study in children with ASD.
source: Functional connectivity was examined using a generalized psychophysiological interaction (gPPI) model within an extended voice processing brain network defined a priori from intrinsic connectivity results described in a previous study in children with ASD (Abrams et al., 2013a) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology and is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The rationale for using an a priori network is it is an established method of network identification that preempts task and sample-related biases in region-of-interest (ROI) selection.
source: The rationale for the use of an a priori network is it is an established method of network identification that preempts task and sample-related biases in region-of-interest (ROI) selection.
evidence: This claim describes the methodological rationale.

claim: The network used in all connectivity analyses consisted of 16 regions.
source: The network used in all connectivity analyses consisted of 16 regions.
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology.

claim: Mothers were instructed to say sentences using the tone of voice they would use when speaking with their child during an engaging and enjoyable shared learning experience.
source: Importantly, mothers were instructed to say these sentences using the tone of voice they would use when speaking with their child during an engaging and enjoyable shared learning experience (e.g. if their child asked them to identify an item at a museum).
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology for stimulus recording.

claim: The three best versions of each nonsense word were selected based on the audio and vocal quality of the utterances.
source: The three best versions of each nonsense word were then selected based on the audio and vocal quality of the utterances (i.e. eliminating versions that were mispronounced, included vocal creak, or were otherwise not ideal exemplars of the nonsense words).
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology for stimulus post-processing.

claim: All participants who participated in the fMRI experiment completed an auditory behavioral test following the fMRI scan.
source: All participants who participated in the fMRI experiment completed an auditory behavioral test following the fMRI scan.
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology.

claim: The goal of the Mother's Voice Identification Task was to determine if the participants could reliably discriminate their mother's voice from unfamiliar female voices.
source: The goal of the Mother's Voice Identification Task was to determine if the participants could reliably discriminate their mother's voice from unfamiliar female voices.
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology.

claim: Each participant was presented with 54 randomly ordered nonsense words: 18 produced by the subject's mother and the remaining 36 produced by unfamiliar female voices.
source: Each participant was presented with 54 randomly ordered nonsense words: 18 produced by the subject's mother and the remaining 36 produced by unfamiliar female voices.
evidence: This claim describes the study methodology.

claim: Vocal samples produced by the participants' mothers were comparable between TD and ASD groups and were similar to the control samples for individual acoustical measures.
source: Acoustical analyses show that vocal samples produced by the participants' mothers were comparable between TD (yellow) and ASD groups (magenta) and were similar to the control samples (cyan) for individual acoustical measures (p>0.10 for all acoustical measures; see Appendix, Acoustical analysis of mother's voice samples).
evidence: This claim is supported by acoustical analysis data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All TD children were able to identify their mother's voice with high levels of accuracy.
source: All TD children and the majority of children with ASD were able to identify their mother's voice with high levels of accuracy, however five children with ASD performed below chance on this measure (see Appendix, Identification of Mother's Voice).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The majority of children with ASD were able to identify their mother's voice with high levels of accuracy.
source: All TD children and the majority of children with ASD were able to identify their mother's voice with high levels of accuracy, however five children with ASD performed below chance on this measure (see Appendix, Identification of Mother's Voice).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Five children with ASD performed below chance on the mother's voice identification measure.
source: All TD children and the majority of children with ASD were able to identify their mother's voice with high levels of accuracy, however five children with ASD performed below chance on this measure (see Appendix, Identification of Mother's Voice).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C.
